chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 251 to 260, Kapilar's kurinji decade on the hill man (குன்றக் குறவன் பத்து): every poem opens on the hill man, his shout, his hut, his sandal fire, his worship and his daughter; the decade moves from praise of the girl as a hill goddess, through the friend's pleas and the household's consent, to the ripened millet that ends the meetings.

251.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the clouds, at the hill man's shout, pour fine and many drops, that the girl weeps even when she only sees the swift-falling cascade that comes down from his town on the tall hill.
251.nuance: The waterfall has done nothing to her: it is only water that has passed his town, and that is enough to make her cry, so the poem measures her longing by the smallest trace of him. The cloud that pours as soon as a hill man calls stands against a lord who does not come though she weeps.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill man, the tall hill and its cascade fix the mountain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the friend speaks of the girl in the third person to the lord (நாட, நும்மூர்), the usual frame for urging him to wed

iraicchi.act: the cloud answers the hill man's shout at once by pouring its rain
iraicchi.sense: in his own land even a cloud answers a call, so the lord who leaves the girl's tears unanswered falls short of his hill's clouds

252.reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the land where young rain-clouds roving over the village common hide the hill man's grass-thatched hut is a noble man: he came back ahead of the great cold north wind of autumn, mixed with sharp dew and driving rain.
252.nuance: He is praised for timing, not for gifts: he came before (முந்து) the cold wind that would have made the waiting unbearable, the kurinji season itself (கூதிர்) being the deadline he beat. The cloud that hides the hut on the common is the only cover the scene gives, and he arrived under it.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill man's hut and the cold season of kurinji fix the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the vocative தோழி and the praise of the man who has come point to the girl; whether he returned from a parting or came to wed the poem does not say

253.reading: The girl asks her friend whether, if the lord of the forest land, where the fragrant smoke of sandal burnt by the hill man perfumes the whole slope, comes to marry her, their mother will consent to the wedding.
253.nuance: வரையின் is both 'of the hill' and 'if he weds': the line can be read as the hill's wedding or as 'if he marries', and either way the question is about the mother, not the man. The smoke that fills the whole mountain from one hill man's fire is a scene, but it is the way a secret spreads.

thinai_evidence.note: sandal burnt on the honey-scented slope fixes the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the vocative தோழி and the anxious question about mother (யாய்) point to the girl in the secret stage

254.reading: The speaker says that the young girl with the bright forehead, around whom bees hum, has been taken by the wealthy ones to their country of hills, a land where the kaanthal smells of the fragrant smoke rising when the hill man cuts the sandal.
254.nuance: The kaanthal takes the scent of the sandal's smoke as the girl now takes the house of the man; the image has only that one correspondence, so it is left as scene. செல்வர் is plural, either honorific for the man or his people who came for her.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal, the sandal and the hill country fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the report that she has been taken (கொண்டனர்) to the man's country reads as the friend telling the foster mother that the marriage has been made; the speaker could also be the foster mother herself

255.reading: The man says that the hill man's beloved young daughter has the grace of the goddesses of the mountain: she is delicate, her breasts have budded, her mouth is red and her chest is spotted with pale gold.
255.nuance: The likeness to the hill goddesses is not flattery alone: in kurinji the அரமகளிர் are the beings who strike men who see them, and the catalogue that follows (budding breasts, the pale spots of a girl newly grown) says she has only just come of age.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain goddesses and the hill man's daughter fix the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: a catalogue of her body in praise is the man's voice; the addressee may equally be his own heart

256.reading: The man says that the hill man's beloved young daughter, the hill girl with bee-haunted hair and a cool leaf skirt, bangled, with teeth bright as sprouts, is young indeed, yet she is a goddess who strikes hard.
256.nuance: ஆயினும் carries the point: her youth (இளையள்) ought to make her harmless, and instead she is ஆர் அணங்கு, a power that afflicts. The fear is the man's, and it is the old fear of a hill goddess, not a figure of speech.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill girl in a leaf skirt fixes kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man explains to his companion why a girl so young has overcome him; the addressee may be his heart

257.reading: The friend tells the man that this bright-bangled young girl, whom the hill man won by worshipping the god and begging, has her long, finely veined eyes flowing with tears, because the land to which he is leaving is far away.
257.nuance: The first two lines set what is at stake: a daughter got by prayer from the god is the treasure the man would leave weeping, so the friend's argument is the father's long begging against the man's short leave-taking. The colophon's kurinji answers the decade's hill people; the situation is a parting.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going to a far land (பிரியும் நாடே) is separation, which decides against the kurinji things

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the friend speaks of the girl to the man who is leaving (நீ பிரியும்), to hold him back

258.reading: Of the hill man's beloved young daughter, the hill girl whose swaying walk is like an adorned peacock's, the friend says that if the lord of the great hill comes to wed her they have given her already, and that is good; yet the girl's grief has not ceased.
258.nuance: கொடுத்தனெம் ஆயினோம் is a past tense for a future act: the household counts her as already given, so nothing now stands between them but the man. The last line turns the good news back on him: consent has not ended her grief, because he has not come.

thinai_evidence.note: the peacock and the great hill fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the friend, speaking for the household (கொடுத்தனெம்), tells the man the way to marriage is open and only his coming is wanting

259.reading: The man says that the one who has stricken him is the hill man's beloved young daughter, who took a few vengai flowers from the village common, praised the mountain god who is the first of her clan, her hands wet and fragrant from making the honey offering, smelling of open kaanthal, her eyes brimming.
259.nuance: The girl who has just worshipped the god of the hill becomes herself the power that strikes him (அணங்கியோள்): the rite and the affliction belong to one vocabulary. Why her eyes brim (கலிழ்ந்த) the poem does not say: it may be her own love she prays about.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai, the kaanthal and the god who lives on the hill fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: எம் அணங்கியோள், she who struck me, is the man's voice; his companion or his heart is the listener

260.reading: The friend tells the man that the soft-shouldered hill girl, the hill man's beloved daughter, will be hard to win now, since they no longer chase the green-backed parrots: the millet sown in the mixed poor ground has ripened.
260.nuance: The harvest is the whole argument: the millet field was the only place the girl could be met, and with the grain ripe she will be kept at home. பெறற்கு அரிது says 'hard to obtain', the language of winning a bride rather than of meeting a lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field and its parrots fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: telling the man that the guarding of the millet is over, so the meetings in the field end, urges him to marry; the man may also be saying it to his heart

links.note: Both have the man, on seeing the girl, take her for an அணங்கு (Kural: அணங்குகொல்; Ainkurunuru: ஆர் அணங்கினளே).
links.teaches: Valluvar's man hesitates between goddess, peahen and woman, while the Sangam man has settled the question and pins it on her youth (இளையள் ஆயினும்), so the couplet's doubt is a refinement of an older certainty that a hill girl can be a striking power.

links.note: 255 says the girl's grace resembles the mountain goddesses (வரையர மகளிர்ப் புரையும்); 256 says she herself is a great அணங்கு.
links.teaches: Two consecutive poems on the same opening line move from likeness to identity, so the decade itself shows a comparison with the hill goddesses hardening into the claim that the girl is one.

links.note: In both the friend (on Parimelazhagar's reading of the Kural) speaks to the man who is about to leave, to hold him back.
links.teaches: The couplet holds the man back with a threat that she will not live, while the Sangam friend holds him back with the girl's worth, a daughter begged from the god, so the pair shows two arguments for the same refusal: her death against her value.

links.note: In 257 the father worshipped the god and begged for the daughter; in 259 the daughter herself worships the clan god of the hill.
links.teaches: Read together the two poems pass the rite from father to daughter: the god who gave her in answer to the father's begging now receives her own offering, made when she has a love of her own to pray for.

links.note: Akananuru 178's friend rejoices that marriage is settled (வரைவு மலிந்து); Ainkurunuru 258's friend says the household has agreed to give her if he weds, yet her grief has not ceased.
links.teaches: Against the friend's joy in Akananuru 178, Ainkurunuru 258 shows that the household's consent alone ends nothing for the girl, so the akam sequence separates the family's yes from the man's coming as two steps.

links.note: Akananuru 28 warns that if the girl does not keep scaring parrots from the millet, mother will set others in her place and his chest will be hard to reach (உறற்கு அரிது); Ainkurunuru 260 says the millet has ripened and the girl is hard to win (பெறற்கரிது).
links.teaches: Akananuru 28 spells out the custom that the Ainkurunuru poem only implies: the girl's freedom lasts exactly as long as the field needs guarding, so 'the millet has ripened' in four lines carries the whole threat of her being kept at home.

links.note: 258 says the household will give the girl if the lord of the hill weds her; 254 says the wealthy ones have taken her to their hill country.
links.teaches: Read against 258's conditional promise, 254 is its fulfilment, so within one decade the hill man's daughter passes from being offered to being carried off to the man's country.
